```{r}
#| label: setup
library(ggplot2)
# Ensure UTF-8 so minus signs and ± render in plots on any machine
utf8 <- isTRUE(l10n_info()[["UTF-8"]])   # fall back to ASCII symbols if R is not running in a UTF-8 locale

oi <- c(blue = "#0072B2", orange = "#E69F00", verm = "#D55E00", green = "#009E73",
        sky = "#56B4E9", purple = "#CC79A7", ink = "#1B1F24", grey = "#4A5560")

theme_jc <- theme_minimal(base_size = 17) +
  theme(
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.caption.position = "plot",
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = oi[["grey"]], size = 10.5, hjust = 0),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_text(colour = oi[["ink"]]),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0, colour = oi[["ink"]]),
    legend.position = "top"
  )

src <- "Source: BALANCE Investigators. N Engl J Med 2025;392:1065-78. Recreated from reported data; not the original figure."
umin <- function(x) if (utf8) gsub("-", "\u2212", x, fixed = TRUE) else x
pm <- if (utf8) "\u00b1" else "+/-"
fmt_rd <- function(rd, lo, hi) umin(sprintf("%.1f (%.1f to %.1f)", rd, lo, hi))

# Primary outcome, Table 2 and Figure 2 of the paper
prim <- data.frame(
  analysis = c("Intention-to-treat (primary)", "Per-protocol", "Modified ITT (alive at day 7)"),
  e7  = c(261, 178, 247), n7  = c(1802, 1370, 1788),
  e14 = c(286, 222, 272), n14 = c(1779, 1483, 1765),
  rd  = c(-1.6, -2.0, -1.6), lo = c(-4.0, -4.5, -3.9), hi = c(0.8, 0.6, 0.7),
  ci_level = c("95.7% CI", "95% CI", "95% CI")
)
prim$rd_check <- round(100 * (prim$e7 / prim$n7 - prim$e14 / prim$n14), 1)
stopifnot(all(prim$rd_check == prim$rd))   # counts reproduce the published differences

# Absolute and relative effects, intention-to-treat
r7  <- prim$e7[1] / prim$n7[1]
r14 <- prim$e14[1] / prim$n14[1]
arr <- r14 - r7                      # absolute risk reduction (14 minus 7)
rrr <- arr / r14                     # relative risk reduction
nnt <- 1 / arr                       # point estimate only
# Published 95.7% CI for difference (7 minus 14): -4.0 to 0.8 percentage points
nntb_limit <- 1 / (abs(prim$lo[1]) / 100)   # benefit end of CI
nnth_limit <- 1 / (prim$hi[1] / 100)        # harm end of CI

# Non-inferiority margin in relative terms
margin <- 4
rel_margin_planned  <- margin / 22                 # planning assumption, 22% control mortality
rel_margin_observed <- margin / (100 * r14)        # observed control mortality
```

## Learning objectives {data-budget="1" data-section="Opening"}

By the end of this session you should be able to:

1. Explain **randomisation, power, confidence intervals** and **intention-to-treat** in plain English
2. Explain how a **non-inferiority** trial differs from a superiority trial
3. Appraise BALANCE with simple checklists and **GRADE**
4. Decide when **7 days** of antibiotics is reasonable for bacteraemia

::: notes
**Say:** Welcome. Today's paper is a large pragmatic RCT that many of us will meet on the next take. Four objectives: learn the key trial words, understand non-inferiority, appraise the trial, and decide whether it should change what we write on the drug chart.

**Timing:** 1 minute (cumulative 1:00). Press T to start the session timer now.

**Approach:** this version is pitched for learners. Each statistical idea gets a tabbed explainer slide (plain English, then BALANCE) followed by a quick quiz. A jargon buster slide sits just before the references as backup.

**Anticipated question:** "Why this paper?" Answer: it applies to almost every specialty that admits patients, the design teaches non-inferiority well, and it is now being cited in local stewardship updates.
:::

## Clinical scenario {data-budget="1.5" data-section="Opening"}

:::: {.card}
**Mrs D, 72.** *E. coli* bacteraemia from pyelonephritis. Admitted to ICU on noradrenaline.

**Day 7:** afebrile for 72 hours, off vasopressors, eating. Switched to an oral agent the isolate is susceptible to.
::::

:::: {.card .orange}
The ward pharmacist asks: **stop today, or complete 14 days?**
::::

::: notes
**Say:** This is a fictional but typical patient. Read the vignette aloud. Ask the room to hold their answer in mind; we will vote on the next slide.

**Timing:** 1.5 minutes (cumulative 2:30).

**Points to draw out:** source is identified and controlled (no obstruction on imaging assumed), organism is not *S. aureus*, she is not severely immunosuppressed and has no prosthetic valve. That places her inside the BALANCE population, which matters later.

**Anticipated question:** "Was the kidney imaged to exclude obstruction or abscess?" Assume yes and no collection. An undrained abscess would have excluded her from BALANCE.
:::

```{=html}
  <div class="poll-row"><button class="poll-btn">Continue to 10 days</button><div class="poll-bar"></div><span class="poll-count">0</span></div>

</div>
```

::: notes
**Say:** Quick show of hands; click each button once per hand to build the bar chart. We will revisit this vote at the end.

**Timing:** 30 seconds (cumulative 3:00).

**Tip:** if the room is large, estimate in fives and click accordingly. Counts reset when the page reloads.
:::

## Why duration matters {data-budget="1.5" data-section="Background"}

::: {.incremental}
- Bloodstream infection: about **2.9 million deaths** a year worldwide [@balance2025]
- Too short: fear of relapse, failure, selection of resistance
- Too long: adverse events, *C. difficile*, resistance in bystander flora, cost
- Guideline durations varied; **14 days or more** was common in critical illness [@balance2025]
:::

::: notes
**Say:** The authors frame the problem as a balance of harms. Early appropriate therapy improves survival, but nobody had shown that the second week adds anything.

**Timing:** 1.5 minutes (cumulative 4:30).

**Source detail:** the 2.9 million figure and the observation that median durations were 14 days or longer in critically ill patients are from the paper's introduction (its refs 2 and 19).

**Anticipated question:** "Isn't 'complete the course' still the message?" Point out that the 'complete the course' message has been challenged in the UK for some years; the aim is the shortest effective course, which is a question of evidence, not adherence.
:::

## Before BALANCE {data-budget="1.5" data-section="Background"}

| Trial | Patients | Population | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| Yahav 2019 [@yahav2019] | 604 | Gram-negative, uncomplicated | 7 d non-inferior |
| von Dach 2020 [@vondach2020] | 503 | Gram-negative, uncomplicated | 7 d non-inferior |
| Molina 2022 [@molina2022] | 248 | *Enterobacterales* | 7 d non-inferior |

: Sample sizes as stated in the BALANCE discussion [@balance2025]

Gaps: few ICU patients, gram-negative only, 10-point margins or composite outcomes.

::: notes
**Say:** Three earlier RCTs all favoured seven days, but they were small, restricted to gram-negative organisms, and either excluded ICU patients or enrolled very few. They used wide margins (10 percentage points) or composite outcomes.

**Timing:** 1.5 minutes (cumulative 6:00).

**Anticipated question:** "So why was another trial needed?" Because a 10-point margin for death is very permissive; BALANCE set 4 points and included ICU and gram-positive infections.
:::

## The clinical question (PICOTT) {data-budget="1" data-section="Background"}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Population

::: {.pico-card .p}
[P]{.letter}

**Hospitalised adults, ward or ICU, with bacteraemia from a pathogenic organism**

- Excluded: *S. aureus* or *S. lugdunensis*, fungaemia, severe immunosuppression
- Excluded: prosthetic valve or endovascular graft, deep or undrained focus
:::

### Intervention

::: {.pico-card .i}
[I]{.letter}

**7 days** of adequate antibiotic therapy

- Drug, dose, route and oral switch chosen by the treating team
:::

### Control

::: {.pico-card .c}
[C]{.letter}

**14 days** of adequate antibiotic therapy

- Identical management to the 7-day arm until day 7
:::

### Outcome

::: {.pico-card .o}
[O]{.letter}

**Death from any cause by 90 days**

- Non-inferiority margin: **4 percentage points** (absolute)
- Secondary: relapse, *C. difficile*, resistant organisms, antibiotic-free days, length of stay
:::

### Question type

::: {.pico-card .t1}
[T]{.letter}

**Therapy**: is a shorter course as safe as the usual course?

- A non-inferiority question, not a superiority one
:::

### Study type

::: {.pico-card .t2}
[T]{.letter}

**Randomised controlled trial**: the best design for a therapy question

- Multicentre, open-label, non-inferiority; 74 hospitals, 7 countries
- Allocation concealed until day 7 of adequate therapy
:::

:::

::: notes
**Say:** Note that 'adequate' means an agent the organism is susceptible to on local laboratory reporting. Drug choice, dose, route and oral switch were left to the treating team. This is a test of a duration strategy, not of a drug.

**Timing:** 1 minute (cumulative 7:00). Click through the six tabs; spend most time on P and O, and use the two Ts to link the question type to the best study design.

**Anticipated question:** "Day 1 counted from when?" Duration was counted as days of adequate treatment; the primary outcome clock started at the date of the index positive blood culture.
:::

## Design and setting {data-budget="1" data-section="Methods"}

- Investigator-initiated, multicentre, **open-label, randomised, non-inferiority** trial
- **74 hospitals, 7 countries**; enrolment October 2014 to May 2023
- Began in ICU only; extended to wards after a parallel ward pilot
- Protocol and statistical analysis plan published before results [@daneman2020protocol]

::: notes
**Say:** Eight and a half years of recruitment, which is itself a teaching point: practice changed over that time (rapid diagnostics, oral step-down).

**Timing:** 1 minute (cumulative 8:00).

**Countries:** the paper lists sites in its Table S1 (supplement), which we did not have. Secondary reports name Australia, Canada, Israel, New Zealand, Saudi Arabia, Switzerland and the USA. [VERIFY against Table S1.] The UK was not a site.

**Anticipated question:** "Who funded it?" Canadian Institutes of Health Research and other public funders in Canada, Australia and New Zealand. All funders listed in the paper are public or charitable research bodies.
:::

## Superiority vs non-inferiority {data-budget="2" data-section="Methods"}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Superiority

::: {.card}
**Question: is the new treatment *better*?**

- Most trials you read ask this
- Example: does a new drug reduce deaths compared with placebo?
- Success = the confidence interval shows a clear benefit (it does not cross "no difference")
:::

### Non-inferiority

::: {.card .orange}
**Question: is the new treatment *not unacceptably worse*?**

- Used when the new option has other advantages: shorter, cheaper, safer, simpler
- We decide in advance how much worse we would tolerate: the **margin**
- Success = the *worst* end of the confidence interval stays inside the margin
:::

### Picture it

```{r}
#| label: plot-ni-explainer
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 3.9
#| fig-alt: "Diagram of four hypothetical trial results against a non-inferiority margin of plus 4 points. Superior: interval entirely below zero. Non-inferior: interval crosses zero but upper end below plus 4. Inconclusive: upper end beyond plus 4. Inferior: whole interval beyond plus 4. BALANCE, minus 1.6 (minus 4.0 to 0.8), is shown as non-inferior."
ex <- data.frame(
  lab = c("Superior (and non-inferior)", "Non-inferior", "Inconclusive", "Inferior", "BALANCE"),
  rd = c(-4.5, -0.5, 1.8, 6.5, -1.6), lo = c(-7, -3, -1.5, 4.8, -4.0), hi = c(-2, 2, 5.3, 8.2, 0.8),
  kind = c("Example", "Example", "Example", "Example", "BALANCE")
)
ex$lab <- factor(ex$lab, levels = rev(ex$lab))
ggplot(ex, aes(rd, lab, colour = kind)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = margin, xmax = 9.5, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = oi[["verm"]], alpha = 0.08) +
  annotate("text", x = 6.8, y = 5.45, label = "7 days unacceptably worse", colour = "#7A2E00", size = 4.6) +
  annotate("text", x = -4.5, y = 5.45, label = "7 days better", colour = oi[["grey"]], size = 4.6) +
  annotate("text", x = 2.05, y = 5.45, label = "7 days a bit worse", colour = oi[["grey"]], size = 4.6) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = oi[["grey"]]) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = margin, linetype = "dashed", colour = oi[["verm"]], linewidth = 1) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), width = 0.2, linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(size = 4, shape = 15) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(BALANCE = oi[["blue"]], Example = oi[["grey"]]), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-8, 9.5), breaks = seq(-8, 8, 2), labels = function(x) umin(as.character(x))) +
  scale_y_discrete(expand = expansion(add = c(0.6, 1))) +
  labs(x = "Difference in deaths, 7 days minus 14 days (percentage points)", y = NULL,
       subtitle = "Dashed line = non-inferiority margin (+4). Grey rows are made-up examples.") +
  theme_jc
```

### Why use it here?

::: {.card .green}
- Nobody expects 7 days to *save* lives compared with 14
- The hoped-for gains are **fewer side effects, less resistance, shorter stays**
- So the fair question is: "Does stopping at 7 days cost lives?"
:::

:::

::: notes
**Say:** Go tab by tab. The key sentence: in a non-inferiority trial, we look at the *worst-case* end of the confidence interval and ask whether it stays within the amount of harm we agreed to accept.

**Picture it tab:** walk down the rows. The 'inconclusive' row is the one people get wrong: the point estimate looks fine, but the interval runs past the margin, so we cannot rule out unacceptable harm. BALANCE is the blue row.

**Timing:** 2 minutes (cumulative 10:00).
:::

## The non-inferiority margin {data-budget="1.5" data-section="Methods"}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### What is it?

::: {.card}
- The **largest amount of extra harm** we would accept in exchange for the benefits of the new approach
- Chosen **before** the trial starts, and written in the protocol
- A smaller margin = a stricter test = needs more patients
:::

### How is it chosen?

::: {.card .orange}
- Clinical judgement: what would patients and clinicians accept?
- Previous evidence about the comparator
- Practicality: tiny margins need enormous trials
:::

### BALANCE: 4 points

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
[+4]{.big-number}

[percentage points of extra deaths: the most BALANCE would accept]{.big-label}
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
[`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * rel_margin_planned)`]{.big-number}

[of the expected 22% death rate with 14 days, in relative terms]{.big-label}
:::
::::

Earlier trials used **10 points**, a much looser test.

:::

::: notes
**Say:** Put it in people terms: a 4-point margin means BALANCE was willing to accept, at most, 4 extra deaths per 100 patients. Ask the room: is that small? It depends on what you gain, and that is a discussion question at the end.

**Calculation:** relative margin = 4 / 22 = `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * rel_margin_planned)`, calculated in R.

**Timing:** 1.5 minutes (cumulative 11:30).
:::

## Quiz: what does non-inferior mean? {.quiz-question data-budget="1" data-section="Methods"}

A non-inferiority trial concludes that 7 days is **non-inferior** to 14 days. This means:

- [A. 7 days is better than 14 days]{data-explanation="Not quite: the answer is C. Non-inferior does not mean better. Showing better needs a superiority result."}
- [B. 7 days is exactly as good as 14 days]{data-explanation="Not quite: the answer is C. Trials cannot prove two treatments are identical; they can only rule out differences larger than a chosen amount."}
- [C. 7 days is not worse than 14 days by more than the agreed margin]{.correct data-explanation="Correct. The worst end of the confidence interval stayed inside the margin, so a large extra harm is unlikely."}
- [D. The trial found no difference, so the result is inconclusive]{data-explanation="Not quite: the answer is C. 'No significant difference' is the language of superiority trials. Non-inferiority asks a different question."}

{{< countdown "0:20" warn_when=5 play_sound="true" bottom="1.4em" >}}

::: notes
**Say:** Start the countdown, show of hands, then select and press A (or click Check).

**Teaching point:** 'non-inferior' is a precise claim: any extra harm is smaller than the margin. It is not 'equivalent' and not 'better'.

**Timing:** 1 minute (cumulative 12:30).
:::

## Who could enter? {data-budget="1.5" data-section="Methods"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Included**

- Admitted when a blood culture grew a pathogenic bacterium
- Ward or ICU
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Excluded**

- *S. aureus* or *S. lugdunensis*; fungaemia
- Severe immunosuppression
- Prosthetic valve or endovascular graft
- Endocarditis, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, undrained abscess
- Single culture with a likely contaminant
:::
::::

::: notes
**Say:** The exclusions remove exactly the groups where we already treat for longer. Keep this list in mind when we discuss applicability; *S. aureus* is the second most common cause of bacteraemia worldwide according to the authors.

**Timing:** 1.5 minutes (cumulative 14:00).

**Detail:** severe immunosuppression was defined as neutropenia, or immunosuppression after solid organ or haematopoietic stem cell transplant.

**Anticipated question:** "Were coagulase-negative staphylococci excluded?" A single positive culture with a common contaminant was excluded. True CoNS bacteraemia could be included, and CoNS made up 4.8% of isolates.
:::

## Randomisation, concealment and blinding {data-budget="1.5" data-section="Methods"}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Randomisation

::: {.card}
**Chance decides who gets which treatment**

- Creates groups that are alike in everything, known *and unknown*, except the treatment
- BALANCE: computer-generated, 1:1, balanced within each **hospital** and for **ICU vs ward**
:::

### Allocation concealment

::: {.card .orange}
**Nobody can know or influence the next allocation in advance**

- Stops clinicians steering sicker patients into one group
- BALANCE: allocation stayed **hidden until day 7**, when the two arms finally differ
:::

### Blinding

::: {.card .purple}
**Who knows which treatment a patient is getting?**

- BALANCE was **open-label** after day 7: no placebo for days 8 to 14
- Analysts were blinded; death is an objective outcome
- Risk: knowing the plan may change behaviour (for example, extending antibiotics)
:::

### What clinicians chose

::: {.card .green}
- Drug, dose, route and oral switch: all left to the treating team
- Adherence checked daily: assigned duration **±2 days**
- A test of a *duration strategy*, not of a particular drug
:::

:::

::: notes
**Say:** Concealment and blinding are often confused. Concealment protects *who gets in which group* (before allocation). Blinding protects *what happens after* allocation. BALANCE has strong concealment and partial blinding.

**Design point:** placebo was not feasible with so many pathogens and regimens. Because both arms are identical until day 7, hiding allocation until then removes early differential management.

**Timing:** 1.5 minutes (cumulative 15:30).

**Anticipated question:** "Was outcome assessment blinded?" Mortality is objective. Adjudication of antimicrobial-resistant organisms and all analyses were blinded to group.
:::

## Quiz: allocation concealment {.quiz-question data-budget="1" data-section="Methods"}

Why did BALANCE keep the allocation hidden until day 7?

- [A. So clinicians could not treat the two groups differently in the first week]{.correct data-explanation="Correct. Both arms get identical care until day 7, so hiding allocation until then prevents early differences in management."}
- [B. To make the trial double-blind throughout]{data-explanation="Not quite: the answer is A. After day 7 everyone knew: the trial was open-label from then on."}
- [C. To make sure the groups were the same size]{data-explanation="Not quite: the answer is A. Group size is handled by 1:1 randomisation in blocks, not by concealment."}
- [D. Because the computer system could not randomise earlier]{data-explanation="Not quite: the answer is A. This was a deliberate design choice, not a technical limit."}

{{< countdown "0:20" warn_when=5 play_sound="true" bottom="1.4em" >}}

::: notes
**Say:** Start the countdown, show of hands, then select and press A (or click Check).

**Teaching point:** good concealment means the people enrolling and treating patients cannot predict or change who goes where.

**Timing:** 1 minute (cumulative 16:30).
:::

## Outcomes and statistics {data-budget="1.5" data-section="Methods"}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Outcomes

- **Primary:** all-cause death by 90 days
- Margin **4 percentage points** (absolute)
- Secondary outcomes exploratory: no multiplicity correction

### Sample size

- 3626 patients for 80% power (explained next)
- One-sided alpha 2.5%, assuming 22% deaths with 14 days
- Three interim looks at the data, so the main result uses a **95.7% CI**

### Analyses

- **Intention-to-treat (ITT)** primary (explained shortly)
- Per-protocol and modified ITT as supporting analyses
- Clustering by centre: separate prespecified mixed model

:::

::: notes
**Say:** A 4-point absolute margin sounds small. In relative terms it is `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * rel_margin_planned)` of the planned 22% control mortality, and `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * rel_margin_observed)` of the observed 14-day mortality of `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * r14)`. Calculated in R from the published figures.

**Timing:** 1.5 minutes (cumulative 18:00). Click through the three tabs.

**Secondary outcomes:** death in hospital and ICU, relapse, adverse events, *C. difficile*, resistant organisms, length of stay, antibiotic-free days and others. No correction for multiplicity; the authors call these exploratory.

**Anticipated question:** "Why both ITT and per-protocol?" In non-inferiority trials ITT can be anti-conservative, so CONSORT asks for both. If they agree, confidence rises.
:::

## Power and sample size {data-budget="1.5" data-section="Methods"}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### What is power?

::: {.card}
**The chance a trial gets the right answer when the answer is "yes"**

- 80% power: if 7 days truly is non-inferior, the trial has an 80% chance of showing it
- Too few patients = low power = a real answer may be missed
:::

### Two kinds of error

| | Truth: non-inferior | Truth: worse than margin |
|---|---|---|
| **Trial says non-inferior** | Correct | **Type I error** (alpha): 2.5% |
| **Trial says not shown** | **Type II error** (beta): 20% | Correct |

: Power = 1 − beta = 80%

### What goes in

::: {.card .orange}
- **Expected event rate** in the comparator group (22% deaths with 14 days)
- **Margin** (4 points): smaller margin = more patients
- **Alpha** (2.5%, one-sided) and **power** (80%)
- Allowance for dropouts and interim analyses
:::

### BALANCE

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
[3626]{.big-number}

[patients planned]{.big-label}
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
[3608]{.big-number}

[patients analysed (intention-to-treat)]{.big-label}
:::
::::

Observed 14-day mortality was **`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * r14)`**, lower than the 22% assumed.

:::

::: notes
**Say:** Power is decided before the trial and depends on four ingredients. BALANCE reached its planned size, so it was not underpowered.

**Type I error in a non-inferiority trial** is the dangerous one: wrongly declaring a shorter course safe. That is why alpha is kept at 2.5% one-sided.

**If asked:** lower-than-expected mortality makes the estimate *more* precise on the absolute scale (fewer events, less variance), so the trial remains well powered, but a fixed 4-point margin becomes relatively larger (`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * rel_margin_observed)` of observed control mortality).

**Timing:** 1.5 minutes (cumulative 19:30).
:::

## Quiz: power {.quiz-question data-budget="1" data-section="Methods"}

BALANCE was designed with **80% power**. What does this mean?

- [A. 80% of patients survived]{data-explanation="Not quite: the answer is C. Power is about the trial's design, not patient outcomes."}
- [B. There is an 80% chance the result is correct]{data-explanation="Not quite: the answer is C. Power is conditional: it applies only if the treatment truly is non-inferior."}
- [C. If 7 days truly is non-inferior, the trial had an 80% chance of showing it]{.correct data-explanation="Correct. Power is the chance of detecting a true effect; the remaining 20% is the type II error rate."}
- [D. 80% of patients followed the protocol]{data-explanation="Not quite: the answer is C. That is adherence, which is a separate issue."}

{{< countdown "0:20" warn_when=5 play_sound="true" bottom="1.4em" >}}

::: notes
**Say:** Start the countdown, show of hands, then select and press A (or click Check).

**Teaching point:** underpowered trials can miss real answers. Always check whether the trial reached its planned sample size.

**Timing:** 1 minute (cumulative 20:30).
:::

## Confidence intervals {data-budget="1.5" data-section="Methods"}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### What a CI shows

::: {.card}
**The range of true effects that fit the data**

- The point estimate is the single best guess
- The interval shows how sure we are: narrow = precise, wide = uncertain
- Bigger trials give narrower intervals
:::

### Reading it

::: {.card .orange}
- **Crosses zero**: we cannot exclude "no difference"
- **Superiority**: whole interval on the benefit side of zero
- **Non-inferiority**: the harm end of the interval is inside the margin
- The interval matters more than the p-value
:::

### Why 95.7%?

::: {.card .purple}
- The data were checked **three times** during the trial (interim analyses)
- Each look "spends" a little of the allowed error (alpha)
- Less is left for the final analysis, so the interval is set at 95.7% to keep the overall error rate at 2.5% one-sided
:::

:::

::: notes
**Say:** One sentence to remember: the confidence interval is the range of true effects compatible with the data. In a non-inferiority trial we care most about the end of that range closest to harm.

**One-sided vs two-sided:** a one-sided test at 2.5% uses the same cut-off as the upper end of a two-sided 95% CI. That is why non-inferiority results are usually shown as a two-sided interval.

**Timing:** 1.5 minutes (cumulative 22:00).
:::

## Quiz: reading the methods {.quiz-question data-budget="1" data-section="Methods"}

Why is the primary result reported with a 95.7% rather than a 95% confidence interval?

- [A. The test was one-sided]{data-explanation="Not quite: the answer is B. The width reflects alpha spent on interim analyses, not sidedness."}
- [B. Alpha was spent on three interim analyses]{.correct data-explanation="Correct. The paper states the 95.7% CI reflects the exact alpha spending incurred in the interim analyses."}
- [C. To correct for prespecified subgroups]{data-explanation="Not quite: the answer is B. Subgroups and secondary outcomes were not corrected for multiplicity."}
- [D. To account for clustering by hospital]{data-explanation="Not quite: the answer is B. Clustering was handled in a separate mixed-model analysis."}

{{< countdown "0:20" warn_when=5 play_sound="true" bottom="1.4em" >}}

::: notes
**Say:** Click the countdown (bottom right) to start 20 seconds, take a show of hands for each option, then click (or press 1 to 4) to select and press A or click Check to reveal.

**Timing:** 1 minute (cumulative 23:00).

**Follow-up:** clustering by centre was handled in a separate prespecified mixed-model analysis, which gave consistent results.
:::

## Intention-to-treat vs per-protocol {data-budget="1.5" data-section="Methods"}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Intention-to-treat

::: {.card}
**"Analyse as randomised"**

- Everyone counted in the group they were assigned to, whatever treatment they actually got
- Keeps the benefit of randomisation: groups stay comparable
- Answers: what happens when we *plan* 7 days in real practice?
:::

### Per-protocol

::: {.card .orange}
**"Analyse those who did as planned"**

- Only patients who received their assigned duration (±2 days)
- Answers: what happens when patients *actually get* 7 days?
- Groups may no longer be comparable (who deviates is not random)
:::

### Modified ITT

::: {.card .purple}
- ITT, but only patients alive on day 7
- In BALANCE, patients who died before day 7 never reached the point where the arms differ
:::

### Why both matter here

::: {.card .green}
- In a **superiority** trial, ITT is cautious: crossover dilutes the difference and makes benefit harder to show
- In a **non-inferiority** trial, the same dilution makes the arms look alike and makes non-inferiority *easier* to show
- So we want ITT **and** per-protocol to agree; in BALANCE they did
:::

:::

::: notes
**Say:** This is the single most important statistical idea for this paper. Use the 'Why both matter here' tab to link back to the 23.9% non-adherence in the 7-day arm, which we will see in the results.

**Timing:** 1.5 minutes (cumulative 24:30).
:::

## Quiz: intention-to-treat {.quiz-question data-budget="1" data-section="Methods"}

Mr K is randomised to **7 days**, but his team keeps antibiotics going to **12 days**. In the intention-to-treat analysis he is counted in:

- [A. The 7-day group]{.correct data-explanation="Correct. ITT analyses everyone as randomised, regardless of what they actually received."}
- [B. The 14-day group]{data-explanation="Not quite: the answer is A. Moving him would break randomisation; that is closer to an 'as-treated' analysis."}
- [C. Neither: he is excluded]{data-explanation="Not quite: the answer is A. Excluding him is what a per-protocol analysis does, not ITT."}
- [D. A separate non-adherent group]{data-explanation="Not quite: the answer is A. Trials do not create new groups after randomisation."}

{{< countdown "0:20" warn_when=5 play_sound="true" bottom="1.4em" >}}

::: notes
**Say:** Start the countdown, show of hands, then select and press A (or click Check).

**Teaching point:** ITT protects randomisation. Per-protocol shows what happens when treatment is actually delivered as planned.

**Timing:** 1 minute (cumulative 25:30).
:::

## Who was randomised? {data-budget="1" data-section="Results"}

```{r}
#| label: plot-flow
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-alt: "Horizontal bar chart of trial flow: 36,637 patients with positive blood cultures were assessed, 13,597 were eligible, 3,631 were randomised, 3,608 formed the intention-to-treat population and 3,581 had complete 90-day outcome data."
flow <- data.frame(
  stage = c("Assessed (positive culture)", "Eligible", "Randomised", "Intention-to-treat", "Complete 90-day data"),
  n = c(36637, 13597, 3631, 3608, 3581)
)
flow$stage <- factor(flow$stage, levels = rev(flow$stage))
ggplot(flow, aes(n, stage)) +
  geom_col(fill = oi[["blue"]], width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(aes(label = format(n, big.mark = ",")), hjust = -0.1, size = 6, colour = oi[["ink"]]) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15)), labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(x = "Patients", y = NULL,
       subtitle = "Of 9,966 eligible but not randomised, 4,532 had an attending physician who declined",
       caption = src) +
  theme_jc
```

::: notes
**Say:** Only 26.7% of eligible patients were enrolled. The largest single reason for non-enrolment was the attending physician declining (4,532 patients). That suggests clinicians kept patients they were worried about out of the trial, a selection effect worth discussing.

**Timing:** 1 minute (cumulative 26:30).

**Numbers:** from Figure 1 of the paper. 1,814 assigned 7 days and 1,794 assigned 14 days in the ITT population; 27 lost to follow-up (0.7%).

**Anticipated question:** "Does low enrolment matter if randomisation was sound?" Internal validity is preserved; external validity (who this applies to) is what suffers.
:::

## Primary outcome: death by 90 days {data-budget="1.5" data-section="Results"}

```{r}
#| label: plot-primary
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| fig-alt: "Forest plot of the risk difference in 90-day mortality, 7 days minus 14 days. Intention-to-treat minus 1.6 percentage points, 95.7% CI minus 4.0 to 0.8. Per-protocol minus 2.0, 95% CI minus 4.5 to 0.6. Modified intention-to-treat minus 1.6, 95% CI minus 3.9 to 0.7. All upper limits lie below the non-inferiority margin of plus 4 points."
pp <- prim
pp$analysis <- factor(pp$analysis, levels = rev(pp$analysis))
pp$lab <- fmt_rd(pp$rd, pp$lo, pp$hi)
ggplot(pp, aes(rd, analysis)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = margin, xmax = 9, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = oi[["orange"]], alpha = 0.18) +
  annotate("text", x = 6.5, y = 3.45, label = "7 days inferior", colour = "#7A5300", size = 5) +
  annotate("text", x = -5.6, y = 3.45, label = "favours 7 days", colour = oi[["grey"]], size = 5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = oi[["grey"]]) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = margin, linetype = "dashed", colour = oi[["verm"]], linewidth = 1) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), width = 0.18, linewidth = 1.1, colour = oi[["blue"]]) +
  geom_point(size = 4.5, shape = 15, colour = oi[["blue"]]) +
  geom_text(aes(x = 9.4, label = lab), hjust = 0, size = 4.6) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-7, 17.5), breaks = seq(-6, 6, 2),
                     labels = function(x) umin(as.character(x))) +
  scale_y_discrete(expand = expansion(add = c(0.6, 0.9))) +
  labs(x = "Risk difference, 7 days minus 14 days (percentage points)", y = NULL,
       subtitle = "Dashed line: non-inferiority margin (+4 points). ITT shows 95.7% CI; other analyses 95% CI", caption = src) +
  theme_jc
```

::: notes
**Say:** 261 of 1,802 died with 7 days (14.5%) and 286 of 1,779 with 14 days (16.1%). Difference −1.6 points, 95.7% CI −4.0 to 0.8. The upper limit is below +4, so non-inferiority is shown. All three analyses agree.

**Timing:** 1.5 minutes (cumulative 28:30).

**Check:** the R code recomputes each difference from the published counts and confirms it matches the published value.

**Anticipated question:** "Does this mean 7 days is better?" No. The interval includes zero, so superiority is not shown. The point estimate favouring 7 days could be chance.
:::

## Absolute effect, calculated {data-budget="2" data-section="Results"}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### BALANCE numbers

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}
[`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * arr)`]{.big-number}

[ARR, percentage points (point estimate)]{.big-label}
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
[`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * rrr)`]{.big-number}

[RRR (point estimate)]{.big-label}
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
[`r sprintf("%.0f", nnt)`]{.big-number}

[NNT (point estimate)]{.big-label}
:::
::::

:::: {.card .orange}
The CI runs from **NNTB `r sprintf("%.0f", nntb_limit)`** through no effect to **NNTH `r sprintf("%.0f", nnth_limit)`**. An NNT is not meaningful when the CI crosses zero.
::::


### What they mean

| Measure | Plain English | BALANCE (ITT) |
|---|---|---|
| **ARR** | Difference in risk: risk with 14 days minus risk with 7 days | `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * r14)`% − `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * r7)`% = `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * arr)` points |
| **RRR** | That difference as a share of the comparator risk | `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * arr)` ÷ `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * r14)` = `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * rrr)` |
| **NNT** | Patients to treat for one extra good outcome: 100 ÷ ARR | 100 ÷ `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * arr)` ≈ `r sprintf("%.0f", nnt)` |

: RRR always looks bigger than ARR; ask for absolute numbers

### Why NNT is tricky here

::: {.card .orange}
- The confidence interval crosses zero: 7 days might be slightly better *or* slightly worse
- So the NNT runs from "benefit" through infinity to "harm"
- In a non-inferiority trial the better question is: **how much harm can we rule out?** Answer: more than about 0.8 extra deaths per 100
:::

:::

::: notes
**Say:** These are calculated in R from the ITT counts (261/1,802 and 286/1,779), not taken from the paper. ARR `r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * arr)` points; RRR `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * rrr)`; NNT `r sprintf("%.1f", nnt)`.

The CI bounds come from inverting the published 95.7% CI limits (−4.0 and +0.8 points). Because the interval crosses zero, the honest expression is 'NNTB `r sprintf("%.0f", nntb_limit)` to infinity to NNTH `r sprintf("%.0f", nnth_limit)`' (Altman's convention).

**Timing:** 2 minutes (cumulative 30:30). Start on 'What they mean' if the room is new to these terms.

**Teaching point:** in a non-inferiority trial the question is not 'how many to treat' but 'how much harm can we exclude'. The data exclude an excess mortality above about 0.8 points with shorter treatment.

**Anticipated question:** "Why not report relative risk?" The trial's margin and analysis were on the absolute scale, which is the scale clinicians and patients use.
:::

## Quiz: number needed to treat {.quiz-question data-budget="1" data-section="Results"}

A treatment lowers the risk of death from **10%** to **8%**. What is the NNT?

- [A. 2]{data-explanation="Not quite: the answer is C. 2 is the absolute difference in percentage points, not the NNT."}
- [B. 20]{data-explanation="Not quite: the answer is C. This is the relative risk reduction (20%), not the NNT."}
- [C. 50]{.correct data-explanation="Correct. ARR = 10% − 8% = 2 points; NNT = 100 ÷ 2 = 50."}
- [D. 80]{data-explanation="Not quite: the answer is C. 80% is the relative risk (8 ÷ 10), not the NNT."}

{{< countdown "0:20" warn_when=5 play_sound="true" bottom="1.4em" >}}

::: notes
**Say:** Start the countdown, show of hands, then select and press A (or click Check).

**Teaching point:** NNT = 100 ÷ ARR (in percentage points). Show the working on the chalkboard (press B) if helpful.

**Timing:** 1 minute (cumulative 31:30).
:::

## Did patients get what they were assigned? {data-budget="1" data-section="Results"}

```{r}
#| label: plot-adherence
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-alt: "Stacked horizontal bars of adherence to assigned duration. 7-day group: 0.8% shorter, 76.1% adherent, 23.1% longer. 14-day group: 5.8% shorter, 83.5% adherent, 10.7% longer."
adh <- data.frame(
  arm = rep(c("Assigned 7 days", "Assigned 14 days"), each = 3),
  cat = rep(c("Shorter than assigned", paste0("Adherent (", pm, "2 days)"), "Longer than assigned"), 2),
  pct = c(0.8, 100 - 23.9, 23.1, 5.8, 100 - 16.5, 10.7)
)
adh$arm <- factor(adh$arm, levels = c("Assigned 14 days", "Assigned 7 days"))
adh$cat <- factor(adh$cat, levels = unique(adh$cat))
ggplot(adh, aes(pct, arm, fill = cat)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6, colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = ifelse(pct > 4, sprintf("%.1f%%", pct), "")),
            position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5), size = 5.5,
            colour = c("white", "white", oi[["ink"]], "white", "white", oi[["ink"]])) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(oi[["purple"]], oi[["blue"]], oi[["orange"]]), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")) +
  labs(x = "Patients", y = NULL,
       subtitle = "Median duration received: 8 days (IQR 7 to 11) vs 14 days (IQR 14 to 15)",
       caption = src) +
  theme_jc
```

::: notes
**Say:** Non-adherence was 23.9% in the 7-day arm (almost all longer courses) and 16.5% in the 14-day arm. Clinicians extended treatment when worried, for example persistent sepsis or a new hospital-acquired infection.

**Timing:** 1 minute (cumulative 32:30).

**Anticipated question:** "Does this undermine the result?" It is the key appraisal issue; we return to it in the quiz on non-adherence. Short version: per-protocol and modified ITT analyses agreed, and a later post-hoc analysis adjusting for non-adherence also agreed.
:::

## Subgroups {data-budget="1" data-section="Results"}

```{r}
#| label: subgroups-data
sg <- data.frame(
  group = c(rep("Severity", 5), rep("Source", 5), rep("Pathogen", 3)),
  sub = c("ICU at enrolment", "Ward at enrolment", "APACHE II 25 or more", "Vasopressor or inotrope", "Clinical Frailty Scale 5 or more",
          "Urinary tract", "Intra-abdominal or hepatobiliary", "Lung", "Vascular catheter", "Unknown source",
          "Gram-positive", "Gram-negative", "Polymicrobial"),
  rd = c(-0.3, -3.2, 0.1, 0.5, 2.8, -1.9, -4.2, 1.5, 2.1, 1.2, 1.6, -2.8, 1.5),
  lo = c(-3.7, -6.3, -7.0, -4.0, -2.1, -5.2, -9.9, -6.1, -8.6, -5.5, -4.5, -5.6, -5.8),
  hi = c(3.1, 0.0, 7.2, 5.1, 7.8, 1.4, 1.4, 9.0, 12.7, 7.9, 7.7, -0.1, 8.7)
)
sg$crosses <- factor(ifelse(sg$hi >= margin, "Upper limit at or beyond +4", "Upper limit below +4"),
                     levels = c("Upper limit at or beyond +4", "Upper limit below +4"))
sg$lab <- fmt_rd(sg$rd, sg$lo, sg$hi)
# One forest plot per subgroup family; shared x-axis so tabs are comparable
plot_sg <- function(g) {
  d <- sg[sg$group == g, ]
  d$sub <- factor(d$sub, levels = rev(d$sub))
  ggplot(d, aes(rd, sub, colour = crosses, shape = crosses)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = oi[["grey"]]) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = margin, linetype = "dashed", colour = oi[["verm"]], linewidth = 0.9) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), width = 0.25, linewidth = 1) +
    geom_point(size = 3.8) +
    geom_text(aes(x = 13.8, label = lab), hjust = 0, size = 4.6, colour = oi[["ink"]]) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(oi[["orange"]], oi[["blue"]]), name = NULL, drop = FALSE) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = c(17, 15), name = NULL, drop = FALSE) +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-10.5, 22), breaks = seq(-10, 12, 2), labels = function(x) umin(as.character(x))) +
    labs(x = "Risk difference, 7 minus 14 days (percentage points, 95% CI)", y = NULL, caption = src) +
    theme_jc + theme(legend.position = "top", axis.text.y = element_text(size = 14))
}
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

Lung, catheter and unknown source cross the plus 4 margin."


### Pathogen

```{r}
#| label: plot-subgroups-pathogen
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-alt: "Forest plot of pathogen subgroups, 90-day mortality risk difference 7 minus 14 days: gram-positive 1.6 (minus 4.5 to 7.7); gram-negative minus 2.8 (minus 5.6 to minus 0.1); polymicrobial 1.5 (minus 5.8 to 8.7). Gram-positive and polymicrobial cross the plus 4 margin."
plot_sg("Pathogen")
```

:::

::: notes
**Say:** Subgroups are broadly consistent, but many intervals are wide and cross the margin, so we cannot claim non-inferiority within them. The authors say as much. Two to watch: frail patients (CFS 5 or more: +2.8, 95% CI −2.1 to 7.8) and lung source (+1.5, −6.1 to 9.0). These are hypothesis-generating only.

**Timing:** 1 minute (cumulative 33:30). Severity tab first (frailty), then Source (lung), then Pathogen (gram-negative).

**Anticipated question:** "Gram-negative looks significantly better with 7 days?" −2.8 (−5.6 to −0.1) just excludes zero, but with 13 or more subgroups and no multiplicity correction, one nominally significant result is expected by chance.

Subgroup values from Figure 3 of the paper; CIs are 95% and unadjusted.
:::

## Quiz: subgroups {.quiz-question data-budget="1" data-section="Results"}

In the gram-negative subgroup, the difference was **−2.8 points (95% CI −5.6 to −0.1)**. What should we conclude?

- [A. 7 days is better than 14 days for gram-negative infection]{data-explanation="Not quite: the answer is B. One of 13 or more unadjusted subgroups reaching significance is expected by chance."}
- [B. It is a hypothesis to test, not a conclusion]{.correct data-explanation="Correct. Subgroups are usually underpowered and not corrected for multiple comparisons; treat them as hypothesis-generating."}
- [C. Gram-positive infections need 14 days]{data-explanation="Not quite: the answer is B. The gram-positive interval is wide and includes no difference; it does not show harm."}
- [D. The overall trial result is invalid]{data-explanation="Not quite: the answer is B. Subgroup findings do not overturn a sound overall result."}

{{< countdown "0:20" warn_when=5 play_sound="true" bottom="1.4em" >}}

::: notes
**Say:** Start the countdown, show of hands, then select and press A (or click Check).

**Teaching point:** the more subgroups you look at, the more likely one 'significant' result appears by chance. Look for consistency with the overall result.

**Timing:** 1 minute (cumulative 34:30).
:::

### Safety and relapse

```{r}

  rd = c(-1.0, -0.6, 0.4, -0.2, 1.1, -0.3, -0.1),

sec$lab <- fmt_rd(sec$rd, sec$lo, sec$hi)
ggplot(sec, aes(rd, out)) +
```

### Antibiotic exposure and stay

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
[19 vs 14]{.big-number}

[Antibiotic-free days by day 28 (median); difference 5 (95% CI 4.6 to 5.4)]{.big-label}
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
[10 vs 11]{.big-number}

[Days in hospital (median); difference −1 (95% CI −1.5 to −0.5)]{.big-label}
:::
::::

:::

::: notes
**Say:** No detectable differences in relapse, *C. difficile*, allergy, AKI or resistant organisms. But these events were rare, so the intervals are wide relative to the event rates. The clear gain is five more antibiotic-free days by day 28, and one fewer day in hospital (median 10 vs 11; difference −1, 95% CI −1.5 to −0.5).

**Timing:** 30 seconds (cumulative 35:00).

**Anticipated question:** "So shorter courses do not reduce resistance?" The trial could not show it: resistance was measured from routine cultures, not active surveillance, and follow-up for *C. difficile* missed community and readmission episodes, as the authors acknowledge.
:::

## Quiz: interpreting the result {.quiz-question data-budget="1" data-section="Results"}

ITT difference −1.6 points (95.7% CI −4.0 to 0.8); margin +4. Which statement is correct?

- [A. 7 days is superior to 14 days]{data-explanation="Not quite: the answer is B. The interval includes zero, so superiority is not shown."}
- [B. 7 days is non-inferior; superiority is not shown]{.correct data-explanation="Correct. The upper limit (0.8) lies below the +4 margin, so non-inferiority is shown; the interval includes zero, so superiority is not."}
- [C. Inconclusive, because the CI crosses zero]{data-explanation="Not quite: the answer is B. Crossing zero is expected; the test is whether the interval stays clear of the +4 margin."}
- [D. 14 days is superior for gram-positive infection]{data-explanation="Not quite: the answer is B. Subgroup results are too imprecise to support this."}

{{< countdown "0:20" warn_when=5 play_sound="true" bottom="1.4em" >}}

::: notes
**Say:** Option C catches people who apply superiority logic to a non-inferiority trial. Crossing zero is expected; the test is whether the interval stays clear of the margin.

**Timing:** 1 minute (cumulative 36:00).
:::

In hospitalised patients with bloodstream infection, "antibiotic treatment for 7 days was noninferior to treatment for 14 days" [@balance2025]

Agree for the **included** population. Caution where excluded or under-represented.

## Appraisal checklists {data-budget="4" data-section="Appraisal"}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### CONSORT (reporting)

[Was the non-inferiority design reported properly?]{.tab-lead}

| Item [@piaggio2012] | BALANCE |
|---|---|
| Margin prespecified and justified | Yes: 4 points, tighter than the 10 points used elsewhere |
| Sample size based on margin | Yes: 3626 planned, 3608 analysed |
| ITT **and** per-protocol reported | Yes, both non-inferior |
| CI interpreted against margin | Yes (95.7% CI) |
| Reference treatment proven effective | No: 14 days is custom, not placebo-tested |

### CASP (quick appraisal)

[A structured set of questions any reader can ask of an RCT]{.tab-lead}

| CASP question [@casp2020] | Judgement |
|---|---|
| Focused question; randomised | Yes |
| All patients accounted for | Yes: 99.3% and 99.2% with day-90 data |
| Blinding | Partial: concealed to day 7, open thereafter; analyses blinded |
| Groups similar at baseline | Yes (Table 1) |
| Treated equally apart from intervention | Unclear: co-interventions not reported |
| Important outcomes covered | Mortality yes; function and patient-reported outcomes no |

### RoB 2 (risk of bias)

[Could the trial's conduct have pushed the result one way?]{.tab-lead}

| Domain [@sterne2019] | Judgement | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Randomisation | [Low]{.rob .low} | Web-based, concealed, balanced groups |
| Deviations from intended intervention | [Some concerns]{.rob .some} | Open-label after day 7; 23.9% vs 16.5% non-adherence |
| Missing outcome data | [Low]{.rob .low} | 0.7% lost to follow-up |
| Measurement of outcome | [Low]{.rob .low} | All-cause death |
| Selection of reported result | [Low]{.rob .low} | Protocol and SAP published in advance |
| **Overall** | [Some concerns]{.rob .some} | Driven by deviations domain |

:::

::: notes
**Approach:** three tools, three questions. CONSORT: was it reported well? CASP: a quick general appraisal. RoB 2: could bias have shifted the result? Spend about 1 minute on CONSORT, 1 on CASP, 2 on RoB 2.

**CONSORT tab.** **Say:** The design is reported well. The last row is the subtle one. Classic non-inferiority logic assumes the comparator has proven efficacy against placebo. Fourteen days has never been shown to beat a shorter course, so the margin is a clinical judgement about acceptable extra deaths, not a fraction of a known treatment effect [@mulla2012].

**Anticipated question:** "Is 4 points small enough?" It is about a quarter of the observed control mortality in relative terms. Would patients accept up to 4 extra deaths per 100 to gain five antibiotic-free days? This is a good discussion point.

**CASP tab.** **Say:** Walk through quickly; most answers are yes. The two weaker areas are the open-label period after day 7 and the lack of information on co-interventions and oral switch timing.

**Anticipated question:** "Could open-label design bias mortality?" Death is objective, so measurement bias is unlikely. The concern is behaviour: clinicians who know the patient will stop at day 7 may look harder for reasons to continue, which feeds the non-adherence issue.

**RoB 2 tab.** **Say:** This is our judgement, not the authors'. The only domain with concerns is deviations. For the effect of assignment (ITT), RoB 2 would often rate deviations that reflect usual practice as low risk. We have been stricter because in a non-inferiority trial, deviations that blur the contrast push towards a finding of non-inferiority.

**Anticipated question:** "Would you rate it high risk?" No. Non-adherence was moderate, the median durations still separated by six days, and the supporting analyses agreed.

**Timing:** 4 minutes (cumulative 40:30).
:::

## Quiz: the non-inferiority trap {.quiz-question data-budget="1" data-section="Appraisal"}

23% of the 7-day group received longer courses. In an ITT analysis of a non-inferiority trial, this tends to:

- [A. Bias towards finding non-inferiority]{.correct data-explanation="Correct. Crossover makes the arms more alike, shrinking any true difference towards zero and so towards non-inferiority. Per-protocol, modified ITT and a post-hoc adjusted analysis all agreed."}
- [B. Bias towards finding inferiority]{data-explanation="Not quite: the answer is A. Crossover makes the arms more alike, pushing towards non-inferiority."}
- [C. Have no effect, because ITT preserves randomisation]{data-explanation="Not quite: the answer is A. ITT preserves randomisation but dilutes the contrast, which is anti-conservative in non-inferiority trials."}
- [D. Raise mortality equally in both groups]{data-explanation="Not quite: the answer is A. Crossover dilutes the difference between arms towards non-inferiority."}

{{< countdown "0:20" warn_when=5 play_sound="true" bottom="1.4em" >}}

::: notes
**Say:** In superiority trials, dilution is conservative. In non-inferiority trials it is anti-conservative. That is why per-protocol analyses matter here.

**Post-hoc analysis** [@ong2026]: non-adherence was associated with prognostic factors (more acute illness, non-urinary source, non-*Enterobacterales* organisms). After inverse probability weighting, the per-protocol risk difference was −1.61% (95% CI −4.13 to 0.87) and the as-treated estimate −0.75% (−3.36 to 1.86), still within the 4-point margin. [VERIFY these figures against the Lancet Infect Dis full text; taken from the published abstract.]

**Timing:** 1 minute (cumulative 41:30).
:::

## Certainty of evidence: GRADE {data-budget="1.5" data-section="Appraisal"}

| Outcome [@guyatt2008] | Certainty | Main reason |
|---|---|---|
| 90-day mortality | **High** | Large trial, precise against margin, consistent with earlier RCTs |
| Antibiotic exposure | **High** | Large, objective difference |
| Relapse | **Moderate** | Imprecision: rare events |
| *C. difficile*, resistance | **Low** | Imprecision; under-ascertainment |

Applies to the trial population; downgrade for indirectness outside it.

::: notes
**Say:** Our GRADE judgement for the question 'in patients like those enrolled'. If you apply it to excluded groups (*S. aureus*, neutropenia, deep foci), indirectness would lower certainty sharply, and in truth the trial gives no evidence for them.

**Timing:** 1.5 minutes (cumulative 43:00).

**Note:** the paper includes a meta-analysis with the earlier trials in Supplementary Figure S1, which we have not reviewed. The 'consistent with earlier RCTs' judgement rests on the three trials summarised earlier.

**Anticipated question:** "Why not downgrade mortality for risk of bias?" The deviations concern was judged not serious because sensitivity analyses agreed.
:::

## Applicability to NHS patients {data-budget="2" data-section="Applicability"}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Likely applies

::: {.card .green}
- Community-acquired gram-negative bacteraemia, especially urinary
- Ward and ICU patients who are improving
- Source identified and controlled
:::

### Uncertain

::: {.card .orange}
- Frail older patients (CFS 5 or more)
- Lung, catheter or unknown source
- Gram-positive organisms other than *S. aureus*
- No UK sites; patients clinicians declined to enrol
:::

### Does not apply

::: {.card .red}
- *S. aureus*, fungaemia
- Neutropenia, transplant
- Endovascular, bone, joint or undrained foci
:::

:::

::: notes
**Say:** Most NHS bacteraemia on the general take looks like the BALANCE population. Uncertainty remains for frail older patients, lung and catheter sources, and gram-positive organisms other than *S. aureus*, where subgroups were small.

**Timing:** 2 minutes (cumulative 45:00). Go through the tabs left to right.

**Selection:** 4,532 eligible patients were not enrolled because the attending physician declined. Patients who worried clinicians may be under-represented.

**Anticipated question:** "What about oral step-down?" Route was at clinician discretion and the paper does not report the oral switch rate in the main text, so we cannot say how much of the 7 days was oral.
:::

## Current guidance position {data-budget="2" data-section="Applicability"}

- **UKHSA Start Smart then Focus (2023):** review at 48 to 72 hours [@ukhsa2023sstf]
- **NHS England:** gives 7 days for gram-negative bacteraemia with urinary source as an example of a shortened course [@nhse2025watch]
- **NICE NG253 (2025)** covers recognition and early management of sepsis; [no NICE recommendation on bacteraemia duration]{.verify} [@nice2025ng253]
- Local trust guidelines set duration: check yours

::: notes
**Say:** There is no national NICE recommendation on how long to treat bacteraemia [VERIFY: confirm that NG253 sections 1.8 and 1.9 do not set a duration]. National stewardship guidance asks us to review at 48 to 72 hours, and NHS England's stewardship report cites seven days for gram-negative bacteraemia with urinary source as a shortened course trusts have adopted. That document is England-specific; colleagues in Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales should check their regional guidance.

**Timing:** 2 minutes (cumulative 47:00).

**Anticipated question:** "Does BALANCE change S. aureus practice?" No. *S. aureus* was excluded and the authors explicitly say their results do not apply to it.
:::

## Discussion questions {data-budget="5" data-section="Discussion"}

1. Would you stop Mrs D's antibiotics today? What would make you extend?
2. Is a 4-point margin for death acceptable? Who should decide?
3. 4,532 patients were kept out by their consultant. Does that change your view?
4. Fixed 7 days or individualised duration?

::: notes
**Timing:** 5 minutes (cumulative 52:00). Spend about 1 minute on each, keep 1 minute in reserve.

**Prompts:**

1. Revisit the poll. Has anyone moved? Reasons to extend: persistent bacteraemia, undrained focus, new infection, not improving by day 7.
2. Patients may weigh antibiotic side effects and length of stay against a small possible mortality risk differently from clinicians. Who sets the margin: trialists, guideline panels, patients?
3. Physician refusal suggests the sickest or most complex patients were selected out, though more than half of enrolled patients were in ICU.
4. von Dach 2020 tested CRP-guided duration [@vondach2020]. The authors call for research on individualised, potentially shorter courses.

**Anticipated question:** "What about day 7 falling at the weekend?" Practical, and real. Stop dates written on day 1 or 3 avoid weekend drift.
:::

## Take-home messages {data-budget="2" data-section="Close"}

::: {.incremental}
- 7 days was **non-inferior** to 14 days for 90-day death: −1.6 points (95.7% CI −4.0 to 0.8)
- **5 more antibiotic-free days**; harms too rare to compare reliably
- Non-adherence biases towards non-inferiority, but supporting analyses agree
- Not for *S. aureus*, severe immunosuppression or deep foci
:::

:::: {.card .green}
**Bottom line:** for improving inpatients with uncomplicated, non-*S. aureus* bacteraemia, plan 7 days and justify anything longer.
::::

::: notes
**Say:** Read the bottom line slowly. That is our interpretation, not the authors' wording.

**Timing:** 2 minutes (cumulative 54:00). Press R to reset the timer for the next presenter.

**Anticipated question:** "Can I quote this to my consultant?" Quote the trial and its population; check that the patient meets the inclusion criteria and that local guidance agrees.
:::

## Jargon buster {data-budget="0" data-section="Backup"}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Non-inferiority

A trial asking whether a new option is **not unacceptably worse** than the standard. Success = the harm end of the confidence interval stays inside the **margin**.

### Margin

The **largest extra harm** we agree in advance to accept. BALANCE: 4 extra deaths per 100.

### ITT / PP

**Intention-to-treat:** analyse everyone as randomised. **Per-protocol:** analyse only those who got the assigned treatment. In non-inferiority trials, check both.

### Power

The chance of showing a true effect. 80% power = a 20% chance of missing it (type II error).

### Alpha

The accepted risk of a false-positive conclusion (type I error). BALANCE: 2.5% one-sided.

### CI

The range of true effects compatible with the data. Narrow = precise.

### ARR / NNT

**ARR:** difference in risk between groups. **NNT:** 100 ÷ ARR (in percentage points).

:::

::: notes
**Backup slide.** Use if a term comes up in discussion. Not timed.
:::
